name: Semaglutide

lead: Semaglutide is a long-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist developed by Novo Nordisk. It is marketed as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for chronic weight management, and it is given as a weekly injection or, in the case of Rybelsus, a daily tablet.

In appearance-focused communities it is used as a fat-loss drug: large reductions in appetite produce substantial total weight loss, and the face usually leans out along with the body. The drug has no known ability to target facial fat specifically; the so-called Ozempic face is generally explained as the effect of rapid overall fat and volume loss, particularly in older people, rather than a distinct action of the molecule.

paras: Semaglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1, binding GLP-1 receptors in the brain's appetite centres and in the pancreas. It reduces hunger and increases satiety, slows gastric emptying, and enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion while suppressing glucagon. A fatty-acid side chain lets it bind albumin, which extends its half-life enough for once-weekly dosing. Weight loss follows mainly from lower energy intake.

Gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are the most common problems, and rarer events include gallbladder disease and pancreatitis. It carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodents. Substantial lean mass can be lost along with fat unless protein intake and resistance training are maintained, and weight is typically regained after stopping. It is prescription-only; compounded and grey-market versions of uncertain quality are widely sold and are a separate safety concern. Facial hollowing and sagging can occur with fast, large weight loss.
